title: The Algorithm as a Human Artifact: Implications for Legal [Re]Search
pub: Law Library Journal, Vol. 109, No. 3 (Summer 2017), pp. 387–422 [2017-20]
author: Susan Nevelow Mart

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the need for selective, human-led deployment and materially develops it with comparative evidence that legal research systems return sharply different results even on controlled searches. It shows why user expertise, redundant search strategies, contextual evaluation and algorithmic accountability are necessary rather than treating any system’s ranked output as generally competent or self-validating.

The answers will allow legal researchers to       be the engaged humans they need to be when working with computer algorithms.

kp.k: Legal search algorithms encode human choices, not neutral judgment
kp.d: Mart argues that legal research is a human interaction mediated by technology: engineers determine stemming, phrase recognition, synonyms, proximity, inclusion and ranking. These choices shape what researchers encounter. The article uses bias primarily to mean a system preference, not necessarily discriminatory or improper behavior, and concerns legal retrieval algorithms rather than generative-AI outputs.
qs: Those human creators made choices about how the algorithm would work that have implications for the search results returned to the researcher.
Once these decisions have been made, searches are auto- matically executed; any bias is encoded into the system.

kp.k: Fifty searches compared six providers' top ten results
kp.d: The study compared Casetext, Fastcase, Google Scholar, Lexis Advance, Ravel and Westlaw using identical keyword searches within reported federal cases in specified jurisdictions: fifty queries, ten results per provider, and 3,000 case results reviewed. Queries were designed as moderately considered starting searches containing multiple words and a legal phrase or concept. Each had to produce at least ten results in every database; fifteen jurisdictional selections changed, three queries were revised and two discarded. The analysis was descriptive, and the selection could favor established concepts and algorithms recognizing unquoted phrases.
qs: The study was expanded to fifty different searches.
Each search had to turn up at least ten
Because not all databases seem to recognize legal phrases with the same consistency, this may have introduced some bias in favor of algo- rithms that recognize more legal phrases without quotes.

kp.k: Identical queries produced substantially different leading cases
kp.d: Across the six providers, the study reports an average of forty percent unique cases in top-ten results and only about seven percent returned by all six. Uniqueness refers to appearance in the compared result sets, not exclusive possession of a case by a database. Mart interprets this variation as evidence that different engineering approaches produce materially different views of similar legal collections.
qs: An average of forty percent of the cases were unique to one database, and only about seven percent of the cases were returned in search results in all six databases.
A fair percentage of cases from each database pro- vider will give a researcher a unique set of cases to look at.

kp.k: Older providers achieved higher measured relevance
kp.d: Table 3 reports top-ten relevance of 39.7% for Casetext, 44.7% for Fastcase, 44.6% for Google Scholar, 57.0% for Lexis Advance, 40.5% for Ravel and 67.0% for Westlaw. Top-five relevance rose to 45.0%, 49.2%, 46.0%, 64.4%, 43.8% and 77.6%, respectively. These are study-specific human judgments of potential usefulness, not recall measures, hallucination rates or contemporary product rankings.
qs: There were more relevant results for the venerable legal database provid- ers LexisNexis and Westlaw, at fifty-seven percent relevance for Lexis Advance and sixty-seven percent for Westlaw
the percentages of cases that are relevant increased slightly for every database, but no one achieved one hundred percent relevance for those cases

kp.k: Relevance results are subjective, time-bound and task-dependent
kp.d: Cases were treated as relevant if potentially worth retaining for later review, including analogical usefulness. Five research assistants independently reviewed five shared, randomly selected queries, yielding moderate agreement: alpha .50 and intraclass correlation .55. Mart warns that different legal objectives or researchers could produce different judgments, and that a percentage measure cannot distinguish two indispensable cases from eight less useful ones without domain expertise.
qs: The importance and immutability of the relevance rankings in this study       must not be overstated.
Different researchers, using the same search       terms, could be trying to solve a slightly different legal problem and could reach       much different determinations of relevance.
To determine relevance at that level of       granularity requires subject expertise in each specific legal domain related to each       search, which was not possible for this study.

kp.k: Search results change beyond additions of new cases
kp.d: A pilot query, 'right to receive information', was repeated across four providers in 2013 and 2016. Mart reports seven new Lexis results despite all existing at the earlier search date, ten new Fastcase results with only two postdating the initial search, three new Westlaw results, and unchanged Google Scholar cases in a different order. This illustrates temporal instability, but Mart explicitly says the single-query comparison is not statistically significant.
qs: This chart illustrates       very clearly that search results change over time by more than the mere addition of       new cases to the database.
But       the results from just one search, while provocative, are not statistically significant.

kp.k: Result volume and case age differed across providers
kp.d: Lexis Advance returned the most results; Google Scholar had the highest proportion of older cases; Westlaw, Fastcase and Casetext returned the most newer cases. Mart reports that average top-ten relevance stayed fairly constant as result volume increased across most databases, while Lexis relevance increased. Case age had no statistically significant relationship with relevance. These observations concern returned results, not complete database coverage.
qs: Lexis Advance returns the highest number of cases
For Lexis Advance, average relevance       actually increases as the number of results increases.
Age of cases did not correlate in any statistically significant way with relevance.

kp.k: Incumbent advantages may reflect accumulated human and user inputs
kp.d: Mart explicitly labels explanations for Westlaw's and Lexis's stronger relevance as speculation. Proposed mechanisms include longstanding classification systems, secondary-source collections, phrase recognition and machine learning from extensive user histories. She reports Westlaw's use of human-generated Key Numbers, headnotes and citation networks, and Lexis's refinement of its topical system with machine learning since 1999. The study does not isolate these mechanisms causally.
qs: There is no way to account for the higher percentages for Lexis and Westlaw       and the clustering effect for the newer database providers, beyond speculation.
It is therefore not that surprising that the legal database providers with the largest user base and the longest search history to mine exhibit one kind of advantage over the newcomers.

kp.k: Classification may constrain which legal arguments become visible
kp.d: Mart argues that legacy classification and differing secondary-source collections embed legal viewpoints in search results. She suggests, rather than demonstrates, that newer providers may escape some nineteenth-century or Langdellian assumptions and surface alternative perspectives or new forms of serendipity. Relevant unique results therefore matter alongside aggregate relevance, especially for emerging legal concepts.
qs: Since the different authorial viewpoints provided by the very different list of secondary sources in Westlaw and Lexis Advance are baked into their respective search results, it is not surprising that the results from Lexis Advance and Westlaw are different.
These classification systems, while not identical, follow a pattern that is familiar to anyone who has taken contracts in law school.
This view is a form of filtering, for better or worse, and the newer legal research databases may be freer of whatever limitations that worldview imposes.

kp.k: Competent research still requires redundancy and human interpretation
kp.d: For practicing lawyers, academics and students, Mart recommends multiple searches and resources rather than reliance on one ranked list. Because lawyers may lack access to every database, they must also vary strategies within available resources. The research studied only a possible first step, not iterative research performance or the effectiveness of supplementary tools. Algorithmic literacy is presented as part of competent research and legal education.
qs: Legal research has always required redundancy in searching; one resource does not usually provide a full answer, just as one search does not provide every       necessary result.
No researcher should stop their       inquiry after just looking at the top ten results from one keyword search.
For attorneys, learning to navigate black boxes is part of the ethical duty to do competent research: knowing something about why you received the results that you did is a critical skill.

kp.k: Transparency should disclose assumptions without exposing proprietary code
kp.d: Mart calls on legal database providers to explain prioritization, classification, association and filtering without surrendering trade secrets. Such information could improve query design, teaching and collection decisions. As a concrete example, she describes Fastcase 7's customizable relevance algorithm, which exposes ranking factors and permits users to change their weights for particular research strategies.
qs: This article argues that legal database providers can be much more transparent about the biases in their algorithms without compromising trade secrets.
Trade secrets should not prevent algorithmic accountability.

Fastcase recently released “Customize Relevance Algorithm,” which allows the researcher to see which factors Fastcase is using in its ranking algorithm and allows researchers to adjust the weights to suit particular research strategies

kp.k: Medicine and automated enforcement illustrate accountability requirements
kp.d: As cross-domain support, Mart reports that doctors using Watson in oncology could inspect underlying evidence and inference paths through Watson Paths, arguing that legal researchers should demand comparable transparency. She also cites an automated speed-enforcement experiment in which three coder groups implementing different instructions produced zero to 661 tickets from the same driving pattern and introduced additional assumptions. These are reported analogies, not findings from her legal-search experiment.
qs: “It’s not sufficient to give a black-box answer,” said Eric Brown, IBM’s       director of Watson technologies.
Legal researchers need to demand the same kind       of transparency.
the number of tickets issued by the algorithms varied from zero to 661, for the same driving pattern.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Mart argues that human-designed search algorithms materially shape which legal authorities researchers encounter, making repeated searches and multiple resources necessary rather than obsolete.
pts.d: The article concerns algorithmic legal information retrieval, including machine learning, rather than contemporary generative AI. Mart reports substantial differences among the top ten results from Westlaw, Lexis Advance, Fastcase, Google Scholar, Ravel, and Casetext. Approximately 40% of results were unique to one database and about 7% appeared across all six. She interprets these differences as evidence that each algorithm embodies a distinct set of human choices. The practical claim is augmentation: researchers must actively formulate, refine, and diversify searches rather than treat ranked results as complete or objective.

pts.k: Mart finds differences in relevance and retrieval profiles across providers, while treating explanations for incumbents' advantages as speculative.
pts.d: Table 3 reports top-ten relevance rates of 67.0% for Westlaw, 57.0% for Lexis Advance, 44.7% for Fastcase, 44.6% for Google Scholar, 40.5% for Ravel, and 39.7% for Casetext. Top-five relevance rates were higher for every provider, but none reached 100%. Mart also reports that Google Scholar returned the highest proportion of older cases, while Westlaw, Fastcase, and Casetext returned more recent cases, and Lexis Advance returned the most results. She suggests that established providers may benefit from classification investments, secondary sources, user histories, and machine learning, but does not establish these as causal explanations. She also suggests that newer providers may offer perspectives less constrained by inherited legal classifications.

pts.k: Mart argues that algorithmic accountability can improve research competence, teaching, and researchers' control over automated retrieval.
pts.d: Mart advocates disclosure of general prioritization, classification, association, and filtering choices without requiring disclosure of proprietary code. Her expected benefits include better query construction, recognition of output limitations, improved research instruction, and better-informed collection decisions. This is a prospective and normative argument, not a measured intervention effect. Watson's visual evidence and inference paths in medicine provide an analogy for transparent assistance to human decision makers, not evidence that a legal AI system has achieved equivalent results.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The central evidence is a descriptive comparison of 50 queries across six databases, involving 3,000 returned case entries and human relevance judgments.
pts.d: Identical keyword queries were applied to jurisdiction-limited sets of reported federal cases intended to approximate the same underlying corpus. Five research assistants assessed relevance using query-specific legal problems and an expansive standard: whether a case might merit further review or contribute by analogy. Five shared, randomly selected queries supported an inter-rater check; the article reports alpha of .50 and intraclass correlation of .55, characterized as moderate concordance. These are human relevance assessments, not generative-model hallucination measurements. Provider materials, correspondence, prior research, and a single-query comparison repeated in 2013 and 2016 supplement the main study. The article explicitly calls its statistical analysis descriptive.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The results are a historically bounded snapshot published in 2017, conditional on the queries, corpus restrictions, interfaces, and subjective relevance standard.
pts.d: Mart explicitly limits interpretation to the algorithms and legal problems in operation when the searches were run. The repeated 2013/2016 example illustrates that results change beyond the addition of newly decided cases, but does not isolate every cause. The main study evaluates only the initial top ten results from deliberately medium-good keyword searches, not complete iterative research or every provider enhancement. Queries had to yield at least ten results in every database; some jurisdictions and queries were revised or discarded. The author acknowledges possible selection bias toward robust search histories and phrase-recognizing algorithms. Coverage was nearly rather than perfectly identical. Relevance judgments did not determine whether a small number of especially important cases outweighed a larger number of generally relevant ones. No forecast date is given for the benefits of greater accountability.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are practicing lawyers, legal scholars, students, research teachers, law librarians, and legal database providers.
pts.d: Lawyers and scholars may miss useful authorities if they rely on one query or one provider. Students need metacognitive skills and practical demonstrations of algorithmic variability; educators and librarians must teach resource and query diversification and consider distinct viewpoints when acquiring resources. Mart links understanding search systems to competent legal research. Access and subscription constraints make effective use of available resources important: Westlaw and Lexis Advance are identified as the most expensive options, with lower-priced or free alternatives also supplying distinctive results. Providers are asked to disclose more about their algorithms; established providers may enjoy data and classification advantages, while entrants may provide alternative perspectives. Clients are affected indirectly through the research used to advise or represent them. The article does not quantify staffing displacement, fee changes, client outcomes, or access-to-justice improvements.
